SCOPING / ENDOSCOPY__Upper GI:
Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD, or gastroscopy) is a flexible endoscopic examination of the upper gastrointestinal tract — the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum — performed via the mouth. It is the first-line investigation for most upper GI symptoms, allows targeted biopsy (e.g. for H. pylori and coeliac disease), and doubles as a therapeutic tool for controlling bleeding, banding varices, dilating strictures and placing feeding tubes.

1Indications — diagnostic & therapeutic

Diagnostic OGD is driven by symptoms and red-flag (ALARM) features; therapeutic OGD is used to intervene directly on bleeding, varices and strictures.

🔬Dyspepsia + ALARMS55
Anaemia, Loss of weight, Anorexia, Recent-onset progressive symptoms, Melaena/haematemesis, Swallowing difficulty, age >55 — 2-week-wait referral
🩸Upper GI bleed
Haematemesis / melaena — diagnostic and therapeutic (within 24h, or immediately after resuscitation if unstable)
🍽️Dysphagia
Any new swallowing difficulty warrants urgent OGD to exclude oesophageal malignancy
🧬Coeliac / IDA
Duodenal (D2) biopsies for villous atrophy; investigation of unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia
🔁Barrett's surveillance
Periodic monitoring of metaplasia for dysplasia / early adenocarcinoma
🛠️Therapeutic
Variceal banding, ulcer haemostasis, stricture dilatation, PEG placement, polypectomy, foreign-body removal
New dysphagia or dyspepsia with ALARM features→Urgent 2-week-wait OGD to exclude upper GI cancer
Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia→OGD (+ colonoscopy) with duodenal biopsy to exclude coeliac and malignancy
2How it is performed

An outpatient day-case procedure using a flexible video endoscope passed under direct vision.

Fasting: nil by mouth for ≥6 hours (clear fluids often allowed up to 2h) to ensure an empty stomach and reduce aspiration risk.
Analgesia/sedation: local anaesthetic throat spray (lidocaine) to the pharynx, with or without IV conscious sedation (midazolam) ± opioid; a mouthguard protects the scope and teeth.
Position: left lateral decubitus, with continuous monitoring of oxygen saturations, and supplemental oxygen given.
Technique: the scope is advanced through the oropharynx, oesophagus, stomach and into the second part of the duodenum; air insufflation distends the lumen and the stomach is retroflexed to view the fundus and cardia.
Sampling: biopsies are taken for histology; antral biopsies for the CLO / rapid urease test detect H. pylori, and D2 biopsies assess for coeliac villous atrophy.
📷 Image placeholder — endoscopic view of the gastro-oesophageal junction showing salmon-pink Barrett's mucosa extending above the gastric folds.
3Key findings & interventions through the scope
🕳️Peptic ulcer
Gastric or duodenal ulcer; risk stratified by Forrest classification for rebleeding
🔥Oesophagitis
Reflux mucosal breaks graded by the Los Angeles (LA) classification A–D
🪱Varices
Oesophageal/gastric varices of portal hypertension — treated by band ligation
🍣Barrett's
Salmon-coloured columnar metaplasia at the GOJ — premalignant, needs biopsy/surveillance
🎗️Malignancy
Ulcerating or fungating mass / stricture — biopsy for diagnosis and staging
💢Mallory-Weiss tear
Linear mucosal tear at the GOJ after retching/vomiting — usually self-limiting
Actively bleeding / visible-vessel ulcer→Dual endoscopic therapy: adrenaline injection PLUS a second modality (clip or thermal) + high-dose PPI
Bleeding oesophageal varices→Endoscopic band ligation + terlipressin + prophylactic antibiotics
Benign peptic stricture / achalasia→Balloon or bougie dilatation through the scope
4Complications, consent & pre-procedure checks
Perforation: the most serious complication — rare in diagnostic OGD but higher with dilatation or stenting; presents with pain, surgical emphysema and sepsis.
Bleeding: especially after biopsy, polypectomy or therapeutic intervention.
Aspiration: gastric contents into the airway, greater with sedation, active bleeding or a non-fasted stomach.
Sedation-related: respiratory depression and hypotension from midazolam — have flumazenil, oxygen and reversal to hand.
Minor: sore throat, bloating and transient discomfort are common and self-limiting.
Pre-procedure preparation→Informed consent, ≥6h fasting, IV access, and check/hold anticoagulants & antiplatelets for therapeutic (high-bleeding-risk) procedures
🚩 PERFORATION and ASPIRATION are the feared complications. Suspect perforation with post-procedure chest/abdominal pain, fever, tachycardia or surgical emphysema — confirm with contrast study/CT and involve surgery early. Adequate fasting and airway vigilance during sedation minimise aspiration; watch for sedation-induced respiratory depression and hypotension.
🎓 In upper GI bleeding, calculate a Glasgow-Blatchford score at presentation to guide admission (a score of 0 may allow outpatient management), then use the Rockall score after endoscopy for rebleeding/mortality risk. Bleeding ulcers should receive dual endoscopic therapy plus high-dose IV PPI.

Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) combines a flexible endoscope with a high-frequency ULTRASOUND probe mounted at its tip. Passed into the GI lumen much like an OGD, it sits the transducer millimetres from the target, giving exquisitely detailed cross-sectional imaging of the individual GI wall layers and the structures immediately adjacent — pancreas, biliary tree, mediastinum and regional lymph nodes. Its proximity to the target gives resolution of the wall layers and small lesions/nodes that far exceeds CT, and a linear echoendoscope lets the operator perform real-time EUS-guided FNA/FNB and therapeutic drainage.

1Indications — staging, characterising & sampling

EUS is primarily a locoregional STAGING and tissue-sampling tool, with a growing therapeutic role.

🔬Cancer staging
Locoregional T- and N-staging of oesophageal, gastric, rectal & pancreatic cancer
🔬Subepithelial lesions
Characterise submucosal masses — GIST, leiomyoma, cyst — by layer of origin
🔬Pancreatobiliary
Assess pancreatic mass, cystic lesions, chronic pancreatitis & biliary strictures
🔬EUS-FNA / FNB
Sample pancreatic masses & mediastinal / peri-GI lymph nodes for cytology/histology
Oesophageal / rectal cancer for curative treatment→EUS defines depth of wall invasion (T) & nodal involvement (N) to guide neoadjuvant vs surgery
Indeterminate pancreatic mass on CT→EUS-FNA/FNB for a tissue diagnosis before oncological treatment

Therapeutic uses (linear scope): EUS-guided drainage of pancreatic pseudocysts and walled-off necrosis, and coeliac plexus block/neurolysis for intractable pancreatic cancer pain.

2How it is performed
Preparation and route mirror OGD (upper GI) or flexible sigmoidoscopy (rectal): fasting, consent, IV access and conscious sedation ± throat spray, left-lateral position.
A radial echoendoscope gives 360° cross-sectional images ideal for staging/orientation; a linear echoendoscope images in the plane of the scope, allowing a needle to be watched in real time for FNA/FNB and drainage.
A water-filled balloon or instilled water improves acoustic coupling to the wall; Doppler identifies intervening vessels before any needle pass.
The normal GI wall is resolved into five alternating layers, letting the operator judge exactly how deep a tumour penetrates.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the endoscopic ultrasound view of the five-layer GI wall with an FNA needle sampling an adjacent node.
3Key findings & interventions
Tumour disrupting deeper wall layers→Higher T-stage — invasion through mucosa/submucosa into muscularis propria or beyond
Round, hypoechoic, well-demarcated node ≥10 mm→Suspicious for malignant node — target for FNA to confirm N-stage
Hypoechoic mass arising from 4th (muscularis propria) layer→Typical of GIST — sample and refer for resection/surveillance by size
Superior resolution of wall layers and small (<1 cm) lesions/nodes compared with CT, allowing accurate early T-staging.
Real-time FNA/FNB yields cytology or core histology from masses and nodes; therapeutic passes create a cystgastrostomy for pseudocyst/walled-off necrosis drainage.
4Complications & safety
Consent for a diagnostic ± therapeutic/sampling procedure, covering the specific FNA risks.
Fasting (typically 6 h food, 2 h clear fluids) to protect the airway during sedation.
Coagulation: check clotting/platelets and manage anticoagulants/antiplatelets before FNA, as needle passes carry a bleeding risk.
Shares OGD complications — perforation, bleeding, infection, and sedation-related aspiration/cardiorespiratory events.
🚩 EUS-FNA/FNB of a PANCREATIC lesion can precipitate acute PANCREATITIS; perforation and bleeding are the other feared complications — safeguard with clotting checks, Doppler vessel-avoidance and appropriate consent.
🎓 EUS is the most accurate modality for locoregional T-staging of GI cancers because the transducer sits directly against the wall — but it is operator-dependent and, unlike CT/PET, does NOT assess distant metastases, so it complements rather than replaces cross-sectional imaging.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) uses a side-viewing duodenoscope passed through the mouth to the second part of the duodenum, where the ampulla of Vater is cannulated, contrast injected and the biliary and pancreatic ducts imaged under fluoroscopy. Once a purely diagnostic test, it is now predominantly therapeutic — MRCP has replaced it for pure imaging — and is the workhorse for relieving biliary obstruction from stones, strictures and cholangitis.

1INDICATIONS — now mainly therapeutic

ERCP is reserved for cases where an intervention is planned. Diagnosis is otherwise done non-invasively with MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound.

🪨CBD stones
Choledocholithiasis — sphincterotomy + balloon/basket extraction
⛔Biliary stricture
Malignant (pancreatic/cholangiocarcinoma) or benign — stenting
🔥Cholangitis
Ascending infection — urgent biliary drainage/decompression
💧Bile leak
Post-cholecystectomy / trauma — stent to divert bile
🧪Pancreatic duct
Strictures, leaks, stones — pancreatic stenting/intervention
🩸Tissue sampling
Brushings/biopsy of indeterminate strictures for cytology
CBD stone on MRCP→Sphincterotomy + basket/balloon extraction
Malignant hilar/distal stricture→Plastic stent or self-expanding metal stent (SEMS)
Charcot triad + obstruction→Urgent ERCP drainage after resuscitation + antibiotics
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Position & anaesthesia: patient prone or semi-prone on the fluoroscopy table, under conscious sedation (midazolam + opioid) or general anaesthesia.
Intubation: the side-viewing duodenoscope is passed to the second part of the duodenum, bringing the ampulla of Vater into view.
Cannulation: the papilla is cannulated with a catheter/sphincterotome and guidewire; contrast is injected and the ducts imaged under fluoroscopy.
Sphincterotomy: the sphincter of Oddi is incised with a diathermy wire to widen the biliary orifice for access.
Clearance/therapy: a balloon or Dormia basket trawls the duct for stones; strictures are dilated and stented (plastic or metal).
📷 Image placeholder — endoscopic view of the ampulla of Vater with sphincterotome cannulating, plus fluoroscopic cholangiogram showing a filling defect (stone) in the common bile duct.
3FINDINGS & THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTIONS

The cholangiogram/pancreatogram is read for filling defects, strictures, dilatation and leaks; therapy follows in the same sitting.

Filling defect in CBD→Stone — extract with balloon/basket after sphincterotomy
Smooth vs shouldered stricture→Benign vs malignant — brush cytology + stent
Contrast extravasation→Bile leak — place stent to decompress and divert
Dilated duct proximal to block→Obstruction confirmed — drain with stent
4COMPLICATIONS & PRE-PROCEDURE SAFETY

ERCP is the most complication-prone routine endoscopic procedure; complications must be consented for explicitly.

🧪Post-ERCP pancreatitis
Commonest & most important — rectal NSAID prophylaxis ± PD stent
🩸Bleeding
Post-sphincterotomy haemorrhage — check coagulation first
🕳️Perforation
Duodenal or retroperitoneal — may need surgery
🦠Cholangitis/sepsis
Introduced infection above an incompletely drained obstruction
💊Sedation/contrast
Cardiorespiratory depression, aspiration, contrast reaction
Consent: explicitly mention post-ERCP pancreatitis, bleeding, perforation and infection risk.
Coagulation: check FBC/clotting; manage anticoagulants/antiplatelets before sphincterotomy.
Antibiotics: give prophylaxis where drainage may be incomplete or in cholangitis/obstruction.
Fasting: nil by mouth (typically ≥6h solids) to reduce aspiration risk under sedation.
🚩 Post-ERCP pancreatitis is the commonest and most feared complication. Give a prophylactic rectal NSAID (PR diclofenac or indometacin) at the time of the procedure, and consider a temporary pancreatic duct stent in high-risk cases, to reduce its incidence and severity.
🎓 MRCP is now the diagnostic test of choice for suspected biliary/pancreatic duct disease; ERCP is reserved for when therapy (stone extraction, stenting, drainage) is intended. Cannulating the ampulla of Vater requires a side-viewing duodenoscope — not the forward-viewing scope used for OGD.

Capsule (wireless video) endoscopy uses a disposable, pill-sized wireless camera that the patient swallows. As it travels passively through the GI tract by peristalsis it captures thousands of images, transmitted to a data recorder worn on a belt. Its chief value is visualising the small bowel — the segment beyond the reach of standard OGD (upper GI endoscopy) and colonoscopy — and it is then passed naturally in the stool.

1INDICATIONS — why look at the small bowel

The dominant indication is obscure GI bleeding or unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia when both OGD and colonoscopy are negative, since the small bowel is otherwise a blind spot.

🩸Obscure GI bleeding
Iron-deficiency anaemia / melaena with negative OGD & colonoscopy — hunt for angiodysplasia, ulcers, tumours
🔬Crohn's disease
Assess suspected or known small-bowel Crohn's (aphthous ulcers, cobblestoning) where no stricture is present
🌾Coeliac complications
Refractory or complicated coeliac disease — ulcerative jejunitis, lymphoma surveillance
🫐Tumours & polyps
Small-bowel tumours and polyposis surveillance, e.g. Peutz–Jeghers syndrome
Anaemia + negative OGD & colonoscopy→Capsule endoscopy to image the small bowel
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Fasting (typically overnight / ~10–12 h) so the mucosa is clean and views are unobstructed.
The patient swallows the capsule with water; sensor leads and a data recorder are worn on a belt to capture the transmitted images.
The patient can usually resume light activity and eat after a couple of hours; the capsule advances passively by peristalsis — there is no sedation and no scope insertion.
Images are reviewed later by the clinician as a video; the capsule is passed naturally in the stool and discarded.
📷 Image placeholder — capsule endoscopy view of small-bowel mucosa showing an angiodysplastic lesion.
3KEY FINDINGS — what you look for
Bright red spider-like mucosal lesion→Angiodysplasia — common cause of obscure small-bowel bleeding
Aphthous ulcers, cobblestoning, skip lesions→Small-bowel Crohn's disease
Mucosal mass or polyp→Small-bowel tumour / Peutz–Jeghers polyp — refer for device-assisted enteroscopy or surgery

A crucial limitation: capsule endoscopy is purely diagnostic. It cannot take biopsies or deliver therapy (no clipping, cautery or polypectomy), and lesion localisation is only approximate — a positive finding usually needs follow-up with device-assisted (double-balloon) enteroscopy.

4COMPLICATIONS & SAFETY

The major complication is capsule retention / impaction: the capsule lodges proximal to a narrowing and can precipitate small-bowel obstruction. It is therefore contraindicated where a stricture or obstruction is known or suspected (e.g. established Crohn's stricture).

Where stricturing is a concern, a dissolvable patency capsule is swallowed first — if it passes intact, the video capsule can safely follow.
Take a careful history for dysphagia or swallowing disorders and prior obstructive symptoms before proceeding.
MRI must be avoided until the capsule is confirmed passed, as it is not MR-safe within the body.
🚩 CAPSULE RETENTION is the key risk — a retained capsule at a stricture can cause small-bowel obstruction requiring endoscopic or surgical retrieval. AVOID capsule endoscopy where stricture/obstruction is known or suspected (e.g. Crohn's stricture); use a patency capsule first. Do NOT perform MRI until the capsule is confirmed passed.
🎓 First-line small-bowel investigation for obscure GI bleeding when OGD and colonoscopy are negative is capsule endoscopy — but always exclude a stricture (patency capsule) first, because retention causing obstruction is the exam's classic complication.

Double-balloon (device-assisted) enteroscopy is a specialised long enteroscope carrying a balloon at its tip, passed through a balloon-fitted overtube. The two balloons alternately inflate and deflate to grip and “pleat” the bowel over the scope, allowing deep intubation of the small bowel far beyond the reach of standard gastroscopy or colonoscopy. Unlike capsule endoscopy, which only takes pictures, it permits BIOPSY and full THERAPEUTIC intervention under direct vision.

1INDICATIONS — diagnostic and therapeutic

It is usually a second-line, targeted tool: capsule endoscopy or cross-sectional imaging flags a lesion, and enteroscopy is then used to reach it to sample or treat.

🩸Obscure small-bowel bleeding
Argon plasma coagulation of angiodysplasia; clipping of bleeding points
🔬Polyps
Polypectomy, e.g. Peutz–Jeghers hamartomas
🎈Strictures
Balloon dilatation of Crohn’s or NSAID strictures
💊Retained capsule
Endoscopic retrieval of an impacted video capsule
🖊️Tattooing
Marking a lesion with ink before surgical resection
🧬ERCP in altered anatomy
Reaching the papilla after Roux-en-Y reconstruction
Capsule shows an actively bleeding angiodysplasia→Enteroscopy to deliver argon plasma coagulation
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — route, sedation and technique

The scope is advanced by a repeated push-and-pleat cycle: advance the scope, inflate its tip balloon to anchor, slide the overtube down and inflate its balloon, deflate the scope balloon, and withdraw both together to concertina the bowel onto the overtube — then repeat.

Antegrade (oral) — reaches the proximal and mid small bowel.
Retrograde (per anum) — passes through the colon and ileocaecal valve to reach the distal ileum.
Combined — both approaches (often with an ink tattoo at the deepest point of the first) to examine the entire small bowel.

It is performed under conscious sedation or general anaesthesia because it is lengthy and uncomfortable; fluoroscopy is sometimes used to confirm scope position.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the endoscopic view / procedure: enteroscope tip and overtube balloons pleating small-bowel loops.
3KEY FINDINGS & interventions through the scope

Under direct vision the operator inspects the mucosa and can act on findings in the same sitting.

Angiodysplasia→Argon plasma coagulation
Peutz–Jeghers polyp→Snare polypectomy
Short fibrotic stricture→Through-the-scope balloon dilatation
Suspicious mass or ulcer→Targeted biopsy ± tattoo for surgery

This is the decisive advantage over capsule endoscopy: capsule is purely diagnostic with no ability to biopsy or treat, whereas balloon enteroscopy can both sample and treat — at the cost of being invasive, time-consuming and requiring sedation or GA.

4COMPLICATIONS & pre-procedure safety

Before the procedure confirm valid consent, appropriate fasting, and review of anticoagulants and antiplatelets (correcting coagulopathy where therapy such as polypectomy is planned).

⚠️Perforation
Higher after dilatation or polypectomy
🩸Bleeding
After biopsy, polypectomy or dilatation
🔥Pancreatitis
Chiefly with the antegrade route — traction on the pancreas
💤Sedation risk
Aspiration and cardiorespiratory events from prolonged sedation/GA
🚩 Perforation and post-procedure bleeding are the major risks, but a complication near-unique to this scope is acute PANCREATITIS after the ANTEGRADE approach, caused by mechanical traction of the pleated bowel on the pancreas — suspect it if there is severe epigastric pain and a raised amylase/lipase afterwards.
🎓 Choose the route by target site: ANTEGRADE (oral) for proximal/mid small bowel, RETROGRADE (per anum) for the distal ileum. If capsule endoscopy localises the lesion, the tattoo left at the deepest antegrade point guides a subsequent retrograde study to complete whole-small-bowel examination.
SCOPING / ENDOSCOPY__Lower GI:
Colonoscopy is flexible endoscopic examination of the entire colon and terminal ileum, passing a video colonoscope from the anus around to the caecum. It is the gold-standard test for investigating lower-GI symptoms and, uniquely, is both diagnostic and therapeutic — the same scope that detects a polyp can remove it, making colonoscopic polypectomy the central colorectal-cancer prevention tool.

1INDICATIONS — diagnostic & therapeutic
🩸Rectal bleeding
Investigate PR bleeding & iron-deficiency anaemia for a source
🔄Change in bowel habit
Persistent change — exclude colorectal cancer
⚠️2-week-wait / +ve FIT
Suspected cancer or positive FIT / bowel-cancer screening
🔁Surveillance
IBD dysplasia & post-polypectomy follow-up
🔬Colitis / IBD
Assess extent & biopsy suspected inflammatory bowel disease
✂️Therapeutic
Polypectomy, haemostasis, dilatation, stenting, decompression
Diagnostic: visualise mucosa, take biopsies, and remove lesions across the whole colon and terminal ileum.
Therapeutic: polypectomy (snare / EMR), haemostasis (clips / APC for angiodysplasia), stricture dilatation, self-expanding metal stenting of obstructing tumours, decompression of sigmoid volvulus or acute pseudo-obstruction, and tattooing lesions for later surgery.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — prep, sedation & technique
Bowel preparation is essential. An oral osmotic laxative (e.g. Moviprep / PEG) is taken the day before to clear the colon — inadequate prep is a leading cause of failed or incomplete examination and missed lesions.
Sedation & analgesia: conscious sedation with IV midazolam plus an opioid (fentanyl / pethidine), or inhaled Entonox, with continuous pulse-oximetry monitoring.
Technique: patient in the left lateral position; the scope is advanced with air/CO₂ insufflation and steering to negotiate the sigmoid and flexures, aiming to reach the caecum and intubate the terminal ileum.
Caecal intubation rate→Key quality marker — target ≥90% confirms a complete exam
Adenoma detection rate (ADR)→Quality marker of thorough mucosal inspection on withdrawal
📷 Image placeholder — describe the endoscopic view of a pedunculated colonic polyp being captured in a snare at colonoscopy.
3KEY FINDINGS & interventions through the scope
Adenomatous / serrated polyp→Snare polypectomy or EMR — prevents progression to cancer
Suspicious mass / ulcerating lesion→Biopsy & tattoo; stage; refer to colorectal MDT
Angiodysplasia / bleeding point→Haemostasis with clips or argon plasma coagulation (APC)
Continuous mucosal inflammation→Biopsy for colitis — assess IBD extent & dysplasia
Obstructing sigmoid volvulus→Endoscopic decompression & flatus-tube placement
Other common findings: diverticulosis, haemorrhoids, and benign strictures.
4COMPLICATIONS & pre-procedure safety
🕳️Perforation
Most serious — risk higher with polypectomy / therapy
🩸Post-polypectomy bleed
May be immediate or delayed up to ~2 weeks
💧Prep effects
Dehydration & electrolyte disturbance, esp. elderly / renal / cardiac
😴Sedation
Respiratory depression, hypotension, aspiration
Consent: document perforation and bleeding risk before the procedure.
Anticoagulation: hold antiplatelets / anticoagulants for planned polypectomy as per protocol to reduce post-polypectomy bleeding.
Renal function: check U&Es before osmotic bowel prep, particularly in elderly, renal or cardiac patients at risk of fluid / electrolyte shifts.
🚩 Perforation and post-polypectomy bleeding are the key serious complications. Suspect perforation with severe abdominal pain, distension, peritonism or free air on imaging after the procedure — and delayed bleeding can present up to two weeks after polypectomy.
🎓 Caecal intubation rate and adenoma detection rate are the headline colonoscopy quality markers. A poor bowel prep is the commonest reason for an incomplete or repeat examination, so always check prep adequacy is documented.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy is an endoscopic examination of the rectum, sigmoid and descending colon using a flexible fibre-optic or video scope, typically reaching as far as the splenic flexure. It is a more limited exam than full colonoscopy, aimed at the distal (left) colon — it lets you inspect the mucosa, take biopsies, snare small polyps and decompress a sigmoid volvulus, but it does NOT visualise the proximal (right) colon.

1Indications — diagnostic & therapeutic

Used when the suspected pathology lies in the rectum or left colon, or as a targeted first look before deciding on full colonoscopy.

🩸Fresh rectal bleeding
Bright red blood thought to be of left-colonic / rectal origin
🚽Distal bowel habit change
New looser stool / tenesmus suggesting left-sided disease
🔬Suspected distal colitis
Assess & biopsy proctitis / define UC extent
🎯Cancer investigation
Part of bowel cancer work-up; historical one-off screening role
🌀Sigmoid volvulus
Endoscopic decompression / detorsion with flatus tube
✂️Tissue sampling
Biopsy & limited polypectomy of distal lesions
Bright red PR bleeding, low-risk, young→Flexi-sig can be the targeted first-line exam
Anaemia / weight loss / FIT-positive high-risk→Colonoscopy needed — flexi-sig alone insufficient
2How it is performed

A key attraction is its simplicity relative to colonoscopy.

Bowel prep: only LIMITED prep needed — typically a single phosphate enema on the day, not full oral bowel-cleansing.
Sedation: often NO sedation required; the patient stays awake, making it quick and suitable for an outpatient / office setting.
Position & route: left lateral position; the scope is passed per rectum and advanced under direct vision with air insufflation.
Extent: rectum → sigmoid → descending colon, reaching roughly the splenic flexure.
📷 Image placeholder — endoscopic view of the sigmoid lumen with a discrete polyp on a haustral fold.
3Key findings & interventions through the scope

You inspect the mucosa for inflammation, mass lesions and vascular abnormalities, and can treat as you go.

Continuous friable granular mucosa from rectum up→Proctitis / ulcerative colitis — biopsy to confirm & grade
Pedunculated / sessile polyp→Biopsy or limited polypectomy (snare)
Irregular ulcerated stricturing mass→Distal colorectal cancer — biopsy & refer
Twisted sigmoid loop / volvulus→Decompression & detorsion, leave flatus tube
Also seen: haemorrhoids, diverticular disease (diverticular orifices, muscular hypertrophy).
Therapeutic scope: biopsy, limited polypectomy, volvulus decompression.
4Complications & safety / pre-procedure requirements

Complications are uncommon and generally fewer than with colonoscopy, but must be consented for.

💥Perforation
Rare but serious; higher with polypectomy / diseased bowel
🩸Bleeding
Mainly post-biopsy / polypectomy; lower risk than colonoscopy
😣Discomfort
Bloating / cramping from air insufflation, usually transient
Consent: informed consent covering perforation, bleeding and missed proximal pathology.
Anticoagulation: check clotting and manage antiplatelets / anticoagulants before planned polypectomy.
Fasting: minimal — usually only a pre-procedure enema; no full fast or sedation recovery needed if unsedated.
🚩 Flexible sigmoidoscopy does NOT visualise the right colon — a right-sided lesion or caecal cancer will be missed. A normal flexi-sig does not exclude proximal cancer in a patient with iron-deficiency anaemia or other high-risk features; these patients need full colonoscopy. If pathology is found or suspicion is high, proceed to colonoscopy.
🎓 Remember the trade-off: flexi-sig wins on convenience — limited enema prep, no sedation, quick and outpatient-friendly — but it is anatomically limited to the splenic flexure. Match the test to the patient: low-risk bright-red bleeding suits flexi-sig; anaemia or systemic red flags mandate colonoscopy.

Proctoscopy and rigid sigmoidoscopy are two simple, rigid, clinic-based instruments for examining the anorectum without sedation. A proctoscope is a short rigid tube that inspects the anal canal and lower rectum — the workhorse for assessing and banding haemorrhoids, and for looking at fissures and other perianal/anal-canal pathology. A rigid sigmoidoscope is a longer rigid scope reaching the rectum and rectosigmoid (up to roughly 20–25 cm), historically used to assess rectal masses, measure the height of a rectal tumour from the anal verge, take rectal biopsies and assess proctitis. Both are quick, cheap, bedside tools needing minimal or no bowel prep (± an enema) and no sedation — but both give a very limited view and cannot exclude disease higher up.

1INDICATIONS — diagnostic & therapeutic

Both instruments target the anorectum. The proctoscope is the anal-canal tool; the rigid sigmoidoscope reaches a little higher into the rectum and rectosigmoid.

🔬Haemorrhoids
Proctoscopy assesses internal piles and allows band ligation
🔬Anal fissure
Visualise the anal canal for a fissure or sentinel pile
🔬Rectal mass
Rigid sigmoidoscopy assesses a palpable/low rectal tumour
📏Tumour height
Measure distance of a rectal cancer from the anal verge
🔬Rectal biopsy
Sample rectal mucosa or a lesion under direct vision
🔬Proctitis
Assess inflamed rectal mucosa (e.g. IBD, radiation)
Bright red rectal bleeding + internal piles→Proctoscopy to confirm and band the haemorrhoids
Low rectal cancer on referral→Rigid sigmoidoscopy to measure height from anal verge for surgical planning
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Position: usually left lateral (Sims) position, knees drawn up; occasionally knee-elbow.
Prep: minimal or none — an enema may be given to clear the rectum; no sedation is required.
Always precede with digital rectal examination (DRE) to check tone, exclude a low lesion and lubricate the canal.
Technique: the lubricated scope is inserted with its obturator/introducer, which is then removed; the instrument is advanced under direct vision, insufflating a little air with the sigmoidoscope to open the lumen.
Proctoscope: withdrawn slowly to inspect the anal canal circumferentially — piles typically at the 3, 7 and 11 o'clock positions.
Rigid sigmoidoscope: advanced to the rectosigmoid; the graduated tube reads the depth in centimetres from the anal verge.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the proctoscopic view of internal haemorrhoids and a rigid sigmoidoscope with its centimetre graduations.
3KEY FINDINGS & THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTIONS
Prolapsing internal haemorrhoids→Rubber-band ligation applied above the dentate line via the proctoscope
Granular, contact-bleeding rectal mucosa→Proctitis — biopsy for IBD / infective / radiation cause
Ulcerated rectal mass at a measured height→Biopsy + record distance from anal verge to guide sphincter-sparing surgery

Therapeutic: the main bedside therapy is haemorrhoid band ligation through the proctoscope. Because banding is applied to insensate mucosa above the dentate line it is generally painless; a band placed too low causes severe pain and must be removed.

4COMPLICATIONS & SAFETY
Minor discomfort and a sensation of wanting to defaecate with air insufflation — usually the only issue.
Bleeding — especially after biopsy or band ligation; secondary haemorrhage can occur a week or so after banding.
Perforation — rare, higher with the rigid sigmoidoscope if forced or over-insufflated.
Vasovagal episode with rectal instrumentation.
Pre-procedure: verbal consent and explanation; review anticoagulants/antiplatelets before biopsy or banding; no fasting or prophylactic antibiotics needed for routine proctoscopy/rigid sigmoidoscopy.
🚩 Proctoscopy and rigid sigmoidoscopy examine ONLY the anorectum — a normal examination does NOT exclude a colorectal cancer higher up. In any patient with red-flag symptoms (change in bowel habit, iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss, higher rectal bleeding), refer for colonoscopy; these scopes are not a substitute for full colonic assessment.
🎓 In rectal cancer, always record the tumour height from the anal verge on rigid sigmoidoscopy: broadly <5 cm = low, 5–10 cm = mid, >10 cm = upper rectum. This distance is decisive in choosing between an anterior resection (sphincter-preserving) and an abdominoperineal resection with permanent colostomy.
SCOPING / ENDOSCOPY__Respiratory / Thora:
Flexible bronchoscopy uses a thin fibreoptic (or video) endoscope passed through the nose or mouth (or via an endotracheal tube) to directly visualise the larynx, trachea and the bronchial tree down to the segmental/subsegmental bronchi. It is both a diagnostic tool — inspecting the airway and obtaining washings, brushings, lavage and biopsies — and a therapeutic one, allowing foreign body retrieval, control of bleeding, clearance of secretions and tumour palliation.

1Indications — diagnostic & therapeutic

The commonest reason is investigation of suspected lung cancer, allowing a central/endobronchial tumour to be seen and sampled. It is also used to work up haemoptysis, persistent unexplained cough, wheeze or stridor, and diffuse lung disease.

🔬Suspected lung cancer
Visualise & biopsy central/endobronchial tumour; washings & brushings for cytology
🩸Haemoptysis
Localise bleeding source; assess airway; potentially control bleeding
🦠Immunocompromised infection
BAL for microbiology, including PCP (Pneumocystis) and atypical organisms
🫁Diffuse lung disease
Transbronchial biopsy & lavage for interstitial/sarcoid pathology
🧩Foreign body
Identify and retrieve aspirated material from the airway
🔎Airway lesion / stenosis
Assess stridor, tracheal/bronchial narrowing, mucosal abnormality
Persistent unexplained cough or wheeze/stridor→Direct airway inspection to exclude tumour, foreign body or stenosis
2How it is performed

The patient is fasted, has SpO₂ monitoring and supplemental oxygen, and usually receives conscious sedation (e.g. midazolam ± an opioid) plus topical local anaesthetic (lidocaine) to the nose, pharynx and vocal cords to suppress the cough and gag reflex.

Route: transnasal or transoral, or through an existing endotracheal/tracheostomy tube in ventilated patients.
The scope is advanced through the cords into the trachea, then systematically inspects the carina and both bronchial trees lobe by lobe.
Continuous oxygen and pulse oximetry throughout; supplemental O₂ titrated to maintain saturations.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the endoscopic view of the carina dividing into the left and right main bronchi.
3Sampling & therapeutic interventions

A range of samples can be taken through the working channel, and several therapies delivered.

Bronchial washings / brushings→Cytology & microbiology from airway surface
Endobronchial biopsy→Histology of a visible central/endobronchial tumour
Transbronchial biopsy→Peripheral/parenchymal lung tissue for diffuse disease (higher pneumothorax risk)
Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL)→Instil & aspirate saline — cell counts, PCP/microbiology in the immunocompromised
Therapeutic: retrieval of an aspirated foreign body.
Therapeutic: control of bleeding (cold saline, adrenaline, tamponade).
Therapeutic: tumour debulking by laser or cryotherapy, and airway stent placement for malignant obstruction.
Therapeutic: clearance of retained secretions and mucus plugs causing lobar collapse.
4Complications & pre-procedure safety

Before the procedure: informed consent, a clotting/coagulation check and review of anticoagulants/antiplatelets (especially if biopsy is planned), fasting, and supplemental oxygen with monitoring in place.

🫁Hypoxia / desaturation
Commonest event — scope & sedation impair ventilation; needs O₂ & SpO₂ monitoring
🩸Bleeding
Especially after endobronchial or transbronchial biopsy
⚠️Pneumothorax
Particularly after transbronchial biopsy — check post-procedure CXR
💨Broncho/laryngospasm
Airway irritation, more likely in asthma/COPD
🌡️Transient fever
Common after BAL; usually self-limiting
💤Sedation-related
Respiratory depression, hypotension — reversible with flumazenil
🚩 The three exam-critical complications are hypoxia, bleeding (worst after biopsy) and pneumothorax. Pneumothorax is classically seen after transbronchial biopsy — obtain a post-procedure chest X-ray to exclude it, and keep supplemental oxygen and monitoring running throughout to guard against desaturation.
🎓 Always check clotting and stop/adjust anticoagulants before any bronchoscopic biopsy. If a patient desaturates after a transbronchial biopsy and becomes breathless with pleuritic pain, think pneumothorax first and get an urgent CXR.

Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) is a bronchoscope with a miniature ultrasound probe at its tip, allowing real-time ultrasound imaging through the airway wall into the mediastinum and hila. A needle can then be passed under continuous ultrasound guidance — EBUS-TBNA (transbronchial needle aspiration) — to sample lymph nodes and masses that sit adjacent to the airways. Its headline role is minimally invasive mediastinal lymph-node staging in lung cancer (N-staging), and it has largely replaced surgical mediastinoscopy for accessible node stations.

1Indications — why EBUS is done

The great strength of EBUS is safely sampling multiple node stations in a single procedure under real-time guidance.

🎯Lung cancer N-staging
First-line sampling of mediastinal & hilar nodes to confirm/exclude nodal spread
🫁Mediastinal mass
Tissue diagnosis of a mass or enlarged nodes of unknown cause
🔬Sarcoidosis
Sampling nodes for non-caseating granulomas when sarcoid suspected
🩸Lymphoma / TB
Nodal sampling for suspected lymphoma or mediastinal tuberculosis
Suspected lung cancer with enlarged/PET-avid mediastinal nodes→EBUS-TBNA to confirm N2/N3 disease before deciding on surgery vs chemoradiotherapy
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in a young adult→EBUS-TBNA seeking non-caseating granulomas of sarcoidosis
2How it is performed
Performed like a bronchoscopy: the scope passes via the mouth (or nose) through the vocal cords into the trachea and main bronchi, under conscious sedation or general anaesthesia with topical airway anaesthesia.
The convex ultrasound probe at the tip is apposed to the airway wall (a saline-filled balloon may aid contact) to image adjacent nodes, which appear as rounded hypoechoic structures beyond the wall.
Colour Doppler is used to identify and avoid intervening vessels (e.g. pulmonary artery) before puncture.
A dedicated aspiration needle is advanced through the working channel and, under continuous real-time ultrasound, passed through the airway wall into the node; suction is applied and several passes taken.
Rapid on-site cytological evaluation (ROSE) may be used to confirm an adequate, diagnostic sample during the procedure.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the endoscopic/ultrasound view: hypoechoic mediastinal node with needle tip advancing across the airway wall under Doppler guidance.
3Node stations, findings & complementary EUS
EBUS reaches the paratracheal, subcarinal (station 7) and hilar/interlobar stations that lie next to the airways, allowing systematic staging across several stations in one sitting.
Cytology/histology is examined for malignant cells (staging), non-caseating granulomas (sarcoidosis), or caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli (TB).
Oesophageal EUS-FNA complements EBUS: performed via the oesophagus, it reaches posterior and inferior mediastinal stations that EBUS cannot, so combined EBUS + EUS maximises staging yield.
Node adjacent to airway (paratracheal, subcarinal, hilar)→Accessible by EBUS-TBNA
Posterior / inferior mediastinal node (e.g. station 8, 9)→Better reached by oesophageal EUS-FNA
4Safety, pre-procedure checks & complications
Consent for the procedure and sedation; fasting (nil by mouth, typically ~6 h solids / 2 h clear fluids) to reduce aspiration risk.
Check coagulation and antiplatelet/anticoagulant status; withhold or bridge agents per local protocol as sampling involves needle puncture.
Complications mirror bronchoscopy and are generally minor: transient hypoxia, cough, sore throat, minor bleeding at the puncture site, and sedation-related effects.
Serious events are rare: mediastinal infection/mediastinitis or abscess, pneumothorax and significant haemorrhage are uncommon; routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not generally required.
🩸Bleeding
Usually minor at needle puncture site; check clotting first
🫁Hypoxia
Transient desaturation during scope passage/sedation
🦠Mediastinal infection
Rare mediastinitis/abscess after nodal puncture
💨Pneumothorax
Uncommon; consider if breathless/desaturating afterwards
🚩 EBUS-TBNA involves passing a needle through the airway wall into the mediastinum — although very safe, watch for the rare but serious complications of significant haemorrhage and mediastinal infection (mediastinitis/abscess); always confirm acceptable coagulation status and anticoagulant management before sampling.
🎓 In lung cancer, EBUS-TBNA is the first-line, minimally invasive test for mediastinal N-staging and has largely replaced mediastinoscopy for accessible nodes — a negative EBUS in high-suspicion cases may still be confirmed surgically. Pair EBUS with oesophageal EUS-FNA to reach posterior/inferior stations and maximise staging accuracy.

Medical thoracoscopy (also called pleuroscopy) is an endoscopic examination of the pleural cavity performed by a respiratory physician, usually under local anaesthetic and conscious sedation, to inspect the parietal and visceral pleura, drain fluid and take pleural biopsies under direct vision. It sits between blind/image-guided biopsy and full surgical VATS: it is far less invasive than video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (which thoracic surgeons perform under general anaesthesia with single-lung ventilation), yet gives direct-vision biopsy with a much higher diagnostic yield than cytology or closed needle biopsy. Its dominant role is investigating an undiagnosed exudative pleural effusion, especially suspected malignancy or tuberculous pleuritis, when fluid cytology is non-diagnostic — and it doubles as a therapeutic tool for drainage and talc pleurodesis.

1Indications — diagnostic and therapeutic

The commonest indication is an exudative effusion that remains undiagnosed after pleural aspiration. Direct-vision parietal biopsy sampling suspicious plaques and nodules gives a diagnostic yield above 90% for malignant and tuberculous disease, well beyond cytology (~60%) or blind Abrams needle biopsy.

🔬Undiagnosed exudate
Cytology-negative effusion needing direct-vision biopsy
🎗️Suspected malignancy
Mesothelioma or pleural metastases — biopsy plus staging
🦠TB pleuritis
Biopsy for granulomas and mycobacterial culture
💧Talc pleurodesis
Poudrage for recurrent malignant effusion
🕸️Empyema/loculation
Breakdown of adhesions and septations under vision
🫁Therapeutic drainage
Complete evacuation with chest drain left in situ
Exudate, cytology non-diagnostic, malignancy suspected→Medical thoracoscopy for direct-vision parietal biopsy
2How it is performed

Performed in an endoscopy suite or theatre with the patient in the lateral decubitus position, affected side up, under local anaesthetic and conscious sedation (surgical VATS instead needs GA and single-lung ventilation).

A single intercostal port is created, typically in the mid-axillary line at the 4th–7th space, guided by prior ultrasound.
An artificial pneumothorax (induced or from the existing effusion) collapses the underlying lung, opening a space to work in.
Fluid is fully aspirated, then the rigid or semi-rigid scope inspects the parietal, visceral and diaphragmatic pleura.
Suspicious areas are biopsied under direct vision; talc poudrage may follow, and a chest drain is left to re-expand the lung.
📷 Image placeholder — thoracoscopic view of the parietal pleura showing scattered nodular tumour deposits with the collapsed lung visible beyond.
3Key findings and interventions through the scope

Direct vision distinguishes appearances that closed biopsy would miss and lets the operator target abnormal pleura.

Nodules or masses on parietal pleura→Suspicious of malignancy — mesothelioma or metastases; biopsy
Diffuse pleural thickening / “candle-wax” nodules→Classical for mesothelioma; sample widely
Sago-grain nodules with adhesions→Tuberculous pleuritis; send tissue for histology and culture
Confirmed malignant effusion→Talc poudrage pleurodesis in the same sitting
Loculations/septations in empyema→Adhesiolysis to create a single drainable cavity
4Complications, contraindications and safety

Pre-procedure requirements: informed consent, correction of coagulopathy and appropriate holding of anticoagulants/antiplatelets, review of imaging (CT/ultrasound) to confirm an accessible pleural space, and IV access with sedation monitoring. The absolute prerequisite is a patent pleural space — if the pleura is obliterated by dense adhesions there is no room to work.

💢Pain
Common; chest drain and pleurodesis discomfort
🫧Prolonged air leak
Persistent bubbling delaying drain removal
🩸Bleeding
Intercostal vessel or biopsy-site haemorrhage
🦠Empyema/infection
Wound or pleural-space infection
🎈Surgical emphysema
Subcutaneous air around the port site
⚠️Organ injury
Rare lung, diaphragm or vessel damage

Contraindications include an obliterated pleural space, uncorrected coagulopathy, and respiratory failure or inability to tolerate lung collapse on the operative side.

🚩 The patient must be able to tolerate collapse of the underlying lung — the induced pneumothorax is deliberate, but in a patient with poor respiratory reserve or contralateral lung disease it can precipitate life-threatening hypoxaemia and haemodynamic compromise. An obliterated pleural space also risks lung laceration on port insertion.
🎓 In a cytology-negative exudative effusion with suspected malignancy or TB, medical thoracoscopy is the investigation of choice: direct-vision parietal biopsy yields >90% versus ~60% for cytology, while blind Abrams needle biopsy is reserved mainly for suspected TB where disease is diffuse.
SCOPING / ENDOSCOPY__Urology:
Cystoscopy is the endoscopic examination of the urethra and bladder using a camera passed per urethra. A flexible scope is a slim, steerable diagnostic instrument used awake in clinic under lidocaine gel; a rigid scope is passed under GA/spinal in lithotomy and permits therapeutic intervention through larger working channels. Its headline role is to exclude bladder cancer (urothelial carcinoma) in a patient with haematuria, but it also enables biopsy, tumour resection, stone retrieval and stent placement.

1INDICATIONS — diagnostic and therapeutic

The dominant indication is haematuria. Visible (frank) haematuria and non-visible haematuria with risk factors both warrant cystoscopy to rule out a bladder tumour.

🔬Visible haematuria
Key indication — exclude urothelial carcinoma
🔬NVH + risk factors
Age ≥60, smoking, occupational exposure
🔬Tumour surveillance
Follow-up of previously resected bladder tumours
🔬Recurrent UTI / LUTS
Assess urethra, prostate, bladder mucosa
🔧TURBT / biopsy
Rigid scope — resect / sample tumour
🔧Stone / stent
Stone removal, retrograde ureteric stent, stricture Rx
Flexible cystoscopy→Diagnostic, awake in clinic under local anaesthetic
Rigid cystoscopy→Therapeutic under GA/spinal — biopsy, resection, stenting
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Flexible: patient supine, aseptic technique, lidocaine gel instilled per urethra as anaesthetic and lubricant; the steerable scope is advanced under direct vision while irrigation fluid distends the bladder.
Rigid: lithotomy position under GA or spinal, aseptic prep and drape; larger instrument gives superior optics and working channels for intervention.
Irrigation fluid (e.g. saline for diagnostic; glycine/water traditionally for monopolar resection) fills and distends the bladder to open the mucosal folds for inspection.
Systematic inspection: examine the entire bladder wall, the trigone, both ureteric orifices (note efflux), the dome and the bladder neck; the urethra and prostate are assessed on withdrawal.
📷 Image placeholder — endoscopic view of a papillary bladder tumour with the ureteric orifice and trigone in the distended bladder.
3KEY FINDINGS & interventions
Papillary / sessile lesion→Suspected urothelial carcinoma — biopsy / TURBT
Bladder stone→Endoscopic fragmentation / retrieval
Erythema / inflamed mucosa→Cystitis — treat cause, biopsy if suspicious
Urethral stricture→Dilatation or optical urethrotomy
Diverticulum→Inspect for stasis, stone or malignancy within

TURBT (transurethral resection of bladder tumour) is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic step for a visible tumour: the lesion is resected with a diathermy loop down to detrusor muscle, providing tissue for staging (T stage) and grade.

4COMPLICATIONS & pre-procedure safety

Before scoping: confirm no active UTI (dipstick/MSU), obtain informed consent, review anticoagulation/coagulation status before any planned intervention, and give antibiotic prophylaxis per local protocol. Rigid work requires fasting for anaesthesia.

🦠UTI / urosepsis
Most feared infective complication
🩸Haematuria
Common after biopsy / resection, usually self-limiting
🔥Dysuria
Transient urethral / bladder irritation
⚠️Urethral trauma
False passage, later stricture
🕳️Bladder perforation
Especially during TURBT
💧TUR syndrome
Hypotonic irrigant absorption → dilutional hyponatraemia
🚩 Never scope through an untreated UTI — instrumentation of infected urine can precipitate urosepsis. Treat active infection first. During TURBT, over-resection risks bladder perforation (watch for an obturator kick and loss of bladder distension).
🎓 Cystoscopy is the essential investigation to exclude bladder cancer in any patient with visible (frank) haematuria — a normal upper-tract image does not remove the need to scope the bladder.

Ureteroscopy (URS) is endoscopic examination of the ureter — and, with a flexible scope, the renal pelvis and collecting system — passed retrograde via the urethra and bladder up the ureter under general or spinal anaesthesia. A rigid/semirigid ureteroscope reaches the distal and mid ureter, while a flexible ureteroscope reaches the upper ureter and inside the kidney (flexible ureterorenoscopy, FURS; retrograde intrarenal surgery, RIRS). Its main role is the diagnosis and treatment of ureteric and renal stones, which are visualised and fragmented with a laser then extracted with a basket — a key stone modality alongside ESWL and PCNL.

1INDICATIONS — diagnostic and therapeutic

The dominant indication is stone disease, but URS is also the workhorse for accessing and treating the upper urinary tract retrogradely.

🪨Ureteric stones
Laser fragmentation + basket retrieval; first-line for many mid/distal stones
🔬Renal stones (RIRS)
Flexible scope for lower-pole / intrarenal stones, esp. <2 cm
🧫Upper-tract UC
Biopsy & treatment of upper-tract urothelial carcinoma
🩸Filling defect / haematuria
Investigate an upper-tract filling defect or localised bleeding
📏Stricture
Assessment ± dilatation of ureteric strictures
Mid/distal ureteric stone not passing→Semirigid URS + holmium laser lithotripsy
Lower-pole renal stone <2 cm→Flexible URS / RIRS as an alternative to ESWL or PCNL
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Performed in theatre under GA or spinal, in lithotomy position, with fluoroscopy available.

Cystoscopy first — the bladder and ureteric orifices are inspected.
Guidewire is passed up the ureter under vision/fluoroscopy to give safe access.
Scope advanced retrograde — semirigid for lower ureter; flexible railroaded over the wire for upper ureter and kidney.
Ureteric access sheath may be placed to ease repeated passage of the flexible scope and lower intrarenal pressure.
Pre-stenting (a JJ stent 1–2 weeks beforehand) is sometimes used to passively dilate a tight ureter.
📷 Image placeholder — endoscopic view of a ureteric stone with a laser fibre and basket, plus a JJ stent in situ.
3KEY FINDINGS & INTERVENTIONS THROUGH THE SCOPE

The operator inspects the ureteric lumen and, with the flexible scope, the whole collecting system, treating pathology directly.

Stone visualised→Fragment with holmium laser lithotripsy, then extract fragments with a basket
Suspicious upper-tract lesion→Biopsy ± laser ablation of urothelial tumour
Ureteric stricture→Balloon dilatation or laser incision
Oedema, bleeding or incomplete clearance→Leave a JJ (ureteric) stent to relieve obstruction

A JJ stent is frequently left afterwards to prevent obstruction from oedema. It causes characteristic stent symptoms: urinary frequency, urgency, haematuria and flank pain (worse on voiding), and must be removed or exchanged within its lifespan.

4COMPLICATIONS & PRE-PROCEDURE SAFETY
🦠Urosepsis
The key risk; treat any UTI before operating
⚠️Perforation / avulsion
Ureteric injury; avulsion is rare but a surgical emergency
📏Stricture
Late scarring of the ureter from injury or inflammation
🩸Bleeding
Usually self-limiting haematuria
🔧Stent symptoms
Frequency, urgency, haematuria, flank pain
🪨Incomplete clearance
Residual fragments may need a further procedure

Pre-procedure requirements: informed consent; treat any active UTI first and give prophylactic antibiotics; check and correct coagulation and stop/bridge anticoagulants as appropriate; and fast the patient for anaesthesia.

🚩 Urosepsis is the most dangerous early complication — never operate on an untreated UTI, and be alert to post-op fever, rigors and hypotension. Ureteric perforation or avulsion is rare but serious: avulsion is a surgical emergency that may require open repair.
🎓 In an infected, obstructed kidney, do NOT attempt definitive stone treatment — decompress first (JJ stent or nephrostomy) and treat the sepsis, then return for laser lithotripsy once the patient is stable.
